description: Symptoms typically begin on lower leaves as small yellow or pale chlorotic dots and flecks that develop into small tan to light-brown lesions with a distinctive diamond shape—an early morphology that is uncommon among other maize foliar diseases. As lesions mature, they elongate into narrow rectangular or brick-shaped spots strictly bounded by leaf veins, measuring roughly 20–30 mm in length and 2–6 mm in width, with darker brown to reddish-brown margins contrasting against tan or pale-tan centers; older dead tissue can fade to creamy white. No sporulation or surface texture is noted, and lesions remain flat and necrotic rather than raised or powdery, helping differentiate this disease from rust or pustule-forming pathogens. The combination of an initial diamond outline transitioning into a vein-limited rectangular or brick-shaped lesion is a key distinguishing feature, particularly separating it from the longer cigar-shaped lesions of Northern Leaf Blight and the raised pustules of rusts. As disease progresses, lesions enlarge and coalesce into extensive irregular necrotic blighted areas, causing premature leaf drying and, in severe cases, canopy-wide blighting. Symptom distribution generally starts on lower leaves and advances upward, with lesions often restricted by leaf veins during early development. In severe or race-specific infections, symptoms may extend beyond the leaf blade to husks, silks, and ear or cob tissue, sometimes producing grey-to-black mold or malformation, and associated stalk weakening can increase lodging risk. Lesion size and shape can vary with pathogen race and host genotype, with some races producing larger, more oval lesions, so morphological variation should be interpreted with appropriate caution during visual identification.

Infection begins as minute pale-yellow to chlorotic flecks on leaf tissue that enlarge into small tan spots which become slightly raised. The most diagnostic feature is the development of circular to oval, sometimes slightly elongated, powdery pustules measuring roughly 0.2–2 mm in diameter that rupture the leaf epidermis and release loose, powdery spores from both the upper and lower leaf surfaces—a bilateral eruptive pattern uncommon among other maize foliar diseases. Pustules progress through a distinctive color sequence: cinnamon-brown, orange-brown, or reddish-brown when actively sporulating, later darkening to dark brown or black as teliospores replace urediniospores, producing a rusty, peppered appearance across the leaf. The raised, blister-like, powdery texture of these lesions—rupturing outward through the epidermis rather than remaining flat or water-soaked—distinguishes them from typical leaf-spot or blight lesions. Pustules are often scattered in patches, but when infection occurs during whorl emergence, they can align in distinct transverse bands across the leaf, an orientation pattern that aids identification. In severe infections, pustules multiply and coalesce into dense clusters or bands, causing yellowing, premature leaf drying, and death of leaves or leaf sheaths, with reduced green photosynthetic tissue overall. Irregular pustule shapes may also appear on midribs or leaf sheaths, and in advanced or heavy infections, symptoms can extend beyond leaves to sheaths, husks, tassels, and stalks. The combination of small powdery pustules present on both leaf surfaces, their characteristic cinnamon-to-reddish-brown coloration maturing to black, and their raised eruptive texture forms the primary basis for distinguishing this disease visually from other maize leaf diseases.

Early infection appears as small pale green or yellowish swellings or localized distortion on young, actively growing tissues, frequently arising at sites of wounding or insect damage. The hallmark diagnostic feature is the development of round, oval, elongated, or irregularly lobed tumour-like galls—a three-dimensional, kernel-shaped swelling rather than a flat lesion, spot, or pustule, sharply distinguishing this disease from all typical maize leaf-spot or blight diseases. Young galls are enclosed by a smooth, distinct membrane and progress in color from pale green or yellow-green to silvery-white or grey-white, then to pale brown as they mature. At maturity, the membrane ruptures to expose a dark brown to black, powdery mass of teliospores inside—an unmistakable internal structural feature not seen in other foliar maize diseases. After spore release, the gall collapses, dries, and leaves behind a dark, shrivelled mass or scar. Galls can form on virtually any above-ground organ, including leaf blades, leaf sheaths, stalks, nodes, tassels, axillary buds, and especially ears, where groups of kernels may become greatly swollen and ear tissue can be partially or extensively replaced by galled masses, sometimes reaching substantial size—markedly larger than galls on leaves or tassels. Secondary distortions include tassel deformation, stalk bending or weakening, reduced fertility, and poorly filled ears in severe cases. The combination of smooth-membraned, silvery-white to grey-white tumour-like galls that rupture to release a black powdery spore mass, occurring on any green tissue but most conspicuously on ears and kernels, constitutes the defining visual signature of this disease.

Early symptoms appear on lower leaves as tiny pinpoint brown, tan, or dark moist-looking spots that are translucent when held against light—a subtle but useful early clue. These progress into the disease's most distinctive feature: long, narrow, sharply rectangular lesions that run parallel to the leaf veins and are strictly bounded by adjacent secondary and tertiary veins, producing a vein-limited, blocky band shape rather than a rounded or irregular spot. Lesions measure roughly 5–70 mm in length and 2–4 mm in width, transitioning in color from translucent to grey, tan, or brown, often edged by a thin yellow chlorotic halo. The lesion surface is moist-looking early on and becomes opaque at maturity, with small dark fungal sporulation points visible within mature lesions—an important confirmatory detail distinguishing it from non-sporulating rectangular lesions of other origins. As disease advances, individual rectangular lesions merge into large, irregular grey-brown blotches, and severely affected leaves blight, dry, and die prematurely; large necrotic areas can encompass much of the leaf blade, sharply reducing photosynthetic tissue. Symptom progression typically begins on lower leaves around flowering and moves upward through the canopy. In severe cases, symptoms may extend to the leaf sheath, and indirect stalk weakening can increase lodging risk. The defining combination for visual identification is the sharply rectangular, vein-limited lesion geometry—long, narrow, grey-to-tan bands running strictly parallel to and bounded by leaf veins—paired with a thin chlorotic halo and dark sporulation points on the mature, opaque lesion surface, differentiating it from cigar-shaped, circular, or pustular lesions seen in other maize foliar diseases.

The earliest sign appears specifically on the youngest, newly expanding leaves as minute pale green, white, or yellow circular flecks, roughly 0.5–2 mm, a distribution pattern that itself is diagnostically useful since older leaves formed before infection remain unaffected. These flecks elongate along secondary and tertiary veins into narrow, fine linear chlorotic streaks that are initially broken and later fuse into continuous, vein-parallel stripes—a symptom pattern distinct from spot- or lesion-forming maize diseases. Streak coloration is characteristically yellow or white, though red or reddish pigmentation may appear in some isolates. The streaks remain flat with no sporulation, pustules, or raised texture, and are strictly vein-limited, running as fine parallel bands rather than expanding laterally across interveinal tissue. In severe cases, streaks fuse and cover much of each newly formed leaf, producing a striped or striated leaf appearance highly distinctive from blight, rust, or gall symptoms. Advanced infection is marked by pronounced systemic effects rather than leaf necrosis alone: severe stunting, shortened leaves and internodes, weak or abnormal growth, curved or abnormal apical/growing-point development, abnormal bunching of shoots or flowers, and small, misshapen, poorly filled, or barren ears. Early infection can result in plant death. The combination of age-dependent symptom expression (confined to leaves emerging after infection), fine chlorotic streaking tightly parallel to secondary and tertiary veins, and pronounced whole-plant stunting with ear malformation forms the key diagnostic signature, clearly differentiating this disease from lesion-, pustule-, or gall-forming maize foliar diseases.

Symptoms occur mainly on older leaves, often concentrated along leaf margins and near veins, beginning as small, light-colored or translucent circular spots that can appear water-soaked when young. The most distinctive diagnostic feature is the development of small round to oval eye-like lesions, only 1–4 mm in diameter, with a tan or cream center encircled by a sharply defined dark ring of red-brown, purple, dark-brown, or black pigmentation, itself often surrounded by a narrow yellow chlorotic halo—a concentric, target-like or frog-eye pattern not seen in other maize foliar diseases. As lesions mature, the necrotic center can collapse and fall out entirely, leaving a characteristic shot-hole appearance in the leaf tissue, a highly distinctive structural sign. Lesions remain flat with no sporulation noted, and are most numerous along leaf margins and adjacent to veins rather than scattered randomly across the blade. In advanced stages, lesions darken further, become fully necrotic, and coalesce into larger irregular dead areas, causing yellowing, premature drying, and death of affected leaf tissue. Severe infections may extend to leaf sheaths and husk leaves covering the ears, causing shrivelling of these structures and, indirectly, reduced grain fill when infection occurs early and heavily. The diagnostic combination of a small eye-like lesion—tan center, dark red-brown to black ring, yellow halo—concentrated along leaf margins and veins on older leaves, frequently progressing to a shot-hole appearance after the center collapses, clearly distinguishes this disease from rectangular, cigar-shaped, streaked, pustular, or gall-forming maize diseases.

Symptoms begin on young leaves as pale green to yellow chlorotic mottling or narrow longitudinal streaks and stripes running parallel to leaf veins. The most distinctive diagnostic feature is the appearance of white, grey-white, or downy fungal growth on the lower leaf surface of these chlorotic stripes, especially visible during humid nights or mornings—a sign not found in bacterial or Cercospora-type leaf-spot diseases and strongly indicative of a systemic pathogen rather than a localized foliar lesion. Stripes are vein-limited and linear, progressing in color from pale green/yellow to yellow-brown, reddish-brown, or necrotic dark brown, and widen over time, merging into larger chlorotic blotches; affected leaves may become narrow, erect, pale, and eventually shredded or torn. Unlike localized leaf-spot diseases, this disease is systemic, and its most pathognomonic features occur beyond the leaf blade: malformed tassels showing leafy proliferation, described as a crazy top appearance, along with excessive tillering and an overall bushy plant habit. Advanced systemic infection produces pronounced whole-plant stunting, malformed or sterile ears with poor grain filling, and can kill seedlings or entire plants before flowering. The combination of parallel-to-vein chlorotic striping with downy sporulation on the lower leaf surface, together with systemic architectural distortions—crazy-top tassel proliferation, excessive tillering, narrow erect leaves, and stunting—forms a highly distinctive diagnostic profile clearly separating this disease from lesion-, pustule-, gall-, or rectangular/cigar-shaped spot-forming maize foliar diseases, where systemic reproductive malformation is not a feature.

Damage appears earliest in the central whorl and newly expanding leaves as fine linear scratches and transparent, elongated window-pane patches where the leaf epidermis has been scraped away, leaving translucent to pale green or yellow-green membranous areas rather than true chlorotic or necrotic lesions—an injury pattern distinct from any fungal or viral leaf symptom. As feeding progresses, these window-pane areas develop into irregular elongated holes and ragged, shredded tears with torn, irregular margins, concentrated deep within the whorl before extending outward to older leaves as feeding continues. A highly distinctive confirmatory sign is the presence of black-brown, sawdust-like frass accumulating within the whorl and leaf axils, along with the causal larva itself, identifiable by a pale inverted Y-shaped marking on the head and four dark spots arranged in a square near the rear. In severe infestations, damage progresses to extensive loss of green photosynthetic tissue or leaf skeletonization, ragged holes coalescing into large areas of missing tissue, and destruction of the central growing point producing a dead heart symptom with dead or torn central leaves. Later-stage or heavier infestations may extend beyond leaves to stem boring (visible stem holes), and injury to tassels, silks, ears, and kernels, often accompanied by heavy frass buildup at these sites. The overall diagnostic picture—mechanical, irregular feeding injury with window-pane translucency, ragged torn margins, whorl-concentrated frass, and a dead-heart symptom—clearly distinguishes this damage from the flat necrotic lesions, pustules, streaks, or galls characteristic of fungal, bacterial, or viral maize diseases.

Early infection appears on lower leaves as small oval to elongated pale green, grey-green, or water-soaked spots that elongate and mature into the disease's most distinguishing feature: long, slender, cigar- or spindle-shaped lesions tapered at both ends, measuring roughly 30–150 mm in length. These lesions run broadly parallel to the leaf veins and leaf margins, giving a linear, vein-aligned orientation rather than a scattered or circular pattern. Coloration progresses from pale water-soaked spots to grey-green, then to tan or straw-colored lesions as they mature. A key diagnostic sign is the dark grey to olive-grey, dusty or sooty fungal sporulation that develops on the lesion surface, most visible on the underside of infected leaves under humid conditions—this sooty texture combined with the elongated cigar shape is highly distinctive. Margins are not sharply delineated by a halo but instead follow the parallel-to-vein orientation, blending into the surrounding leaf tissue as lesions mature. In advanced stages, individual lesions enlarge and coalesce into irregular, larger areas of dead, straw-tan tissue, producing extensive leaf blighting, drying, and brittleness; severe cases can resemble frost damage due to the widespread scorched appearance. Disease progression is typically vertical, beginning on lower/older leaves and moving upward through the canopy over time, though late-season infections may appear throughout the plant. In susceptible cultivars under severe pressure, symptoms may extend to the husk or ear covering. The combination of long, tapered, cigar-shaped lesions running parallel to leaf veins, straw-tan coloration, and dark sooty sporulation on lesion undersides is the most reliable visual signature for distinguishing this disease from other maize foliar diseases with rounder, smaller, or halo-bearing lesions.
